why: 'At least minDistance apart' is about shortest-road distance, so Dijkstra gives every distance you need. Run a multi-source Dijkstra from each company's centers (at most 10), mark which company pairs and which single companies are too close, then try all 2^10 subsets.
hints: There are at most 10 companies, so once you know which pairs of companies clash, checking all 1,023 non-empty subsets is cheap. The hard part is the distances.

Run one multi-source Dijkstra per company, starting from all of its centers at distance 0. Any center of another company reached at distance < minDistance makes that pair of companies incompatible. A company can also clash with itself if two of its own centers are too close.

For the self check, record which source each node was reached from; an edge (u, v, w) whose endpoints came from different sources of the same company gives a candidate distance dist[u] + w + dist[v]. You can stop each Dijkstra once distances reach minDistance. That is about 10 Dijkstras in O(E log V), then 2^k x k^2 for the subsets.
pitfalls: Two centers owned by the same company must also be at least minDistance apart, or that company can never be contracted.
Use the shortest path, not the direct road: in the example the road 1-3 has length 5, and the detour 1-2-3 also has length 5.
Centers that cannot reach each other at all are infinitely far apart, so they never clash.
The empty subset does not count.
statement:
An e-commerce company wants to contract local businesses to use their stores as pick-up and drop-off centers (pdcs). The city is a weighted, undirected graph: nodes 1..n are the potential pdcs, and each edge graphFrom[i] - graphTo[i] is a road of length graphWeight[i].

Each pdc is owned by one company: node i + 1 belongs to company company[i]. Contracting a company means using all of its pdcs.

A set of companies is valid if every two pdcs it uses (including two pdcs of the same company) are at least minDistance apart, measured by shortest road distance. Pdcs that cannot reach each other are far enough apart.

Return the number of non-empty valid sets of companies.

Example: n = 3, roads 1-2 (3), 2-3 (2), 3-1 (5), minDistance = 4, company = [1, 2, 3].

  1. Shortest distances: d(1,2) = 3, d(2,3) = 2, d(1,3) = min(5, 3 + 2) = 5.
  2. Only the pair (1, 3) is at least 4 apart, so companies 1 and 2 clash and companies 2 and 3 clash.
  3. Valid sets: {1}, {2}, {3}, {1, 3}.

The answer is 4.
constraints:
• 2 <= n <= 1000 (nodes)
  • 1 <= number of roads <= min(1000, n(n-1)/2)
  • 1 <= graphWeight[i] <= 1000
  • 1 <= minDistance <= 100
  • 1 <= company[i] <= 10
  • No self-loops and at most one road between any two nodes.
